subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 8 periods = 320 minutes
Total: 8 periods · 5h 20min

periods.activity_title: Pouring and Comparing: Which Glass Holds More?

tasks_in_class.description: Who drank the most milk? Who drank the least milk? (from the picture of three glasses poured into same-sized glasses)
Get three vessels (small bowl, glass, bottle) from home; guess how many small bowls fill each; pour water from one vessel into another to check.
Fill in the blanks with 'the most' or 'the least': the glass holds ___ water; the bottle holds ___ water.

homework.description: Fill in the blanks with 'more' or 'less': Nita's glass holds ___ milk than Monu's; Monu's holds ___ than Nita's; Ritu's holds ___ than Nita's.

time_bands.activity: Open with the story of Ritu, Monu, and Nita. Display three differently shaped vessels and ask: 'Can we tell just by looking which holds more?' Pour the contents of each into same-sized glasses as the children watch, so they see that appearance alone is misleading.

Work through Let us Discuss Q1–2, p.140 ("Who drank the most milk? Who drank the least milk?...") as a whole-class discussion, inviting children to explain how they can tell from the same-sized-glass picture.

Move into the vessel activity — Let us Do (vessel activity), p.141 ("Get three vessels…pour water from one vessel into another to check....") — in small groups. Children first guess how many small bowls fill the glass, then the bottle, recording guesses before pouring to verify.

Whole-class share-out: groups report their guesses versus the pour results. Consolidate with Let us Do Q1(a–b), p.141 ("Fill in the blanks with 'the most' or 'the least'...."), children completing the blanks based on what the class found.

periods.teacher_notes: Children often assume the tallest vessel holds the most; the same-sized-glass pour is the key move that breaks this assumption. Note T-3 and T-6 are close complements of T-1 and T-5 respectively; they are suitable as additional practice: Let us Do Q4(a–b) and Q2, p.141. A common error is to confuse the height of the liquid with the total capacity of the vessel — redirect by asking 'But what if the vessel is very wide?'
materials: Three vessels of different shapes and sizes (bowl, glass, bottle)
Same-sized transparent cups for pouring comparison
Recording sheet or slate for guessing

periods.activity_title: Meet the Litre: A Standard for Capacity

tasks_in_class.description: How many ladles fill the bowl? How many glasses can be filled by the jug? (from the lemonade stall picture)
Tick the appropriate word: the glass holds more than/less than 1 litre; the bowl holds more than/less than 1 litre; the jug holds more than/less than/exactly 1 litre.
Find vessels at home that are exactly 1 litre using the 1 litre bottle to check; identify vessels that are more than or less than 1 litre.

homework.description: How many glasses can be filled with 3 jugs of lemonade?

time_bands.activity: Display the lemonade stall picture and pose Let us Do Q1–2, p.142 ("How many ladles fill the bowl? How many glasses can be filled by the jug?..."). Children examine the picture in pairs and record answers; discuss as a class, emphasising that informal units (ladle, glass) give different counts.

Introduce the 1-litre bottle as a standard reference. Show children the bottle and pour into a glass, a bowl, and a jug in turn. Work through Let us Discuss Q1(a–c), p.143 ("Tick the appropriate word: the glass holds more than/less than 1 litre....") as a guided class exercise, with children predicting before the pour.

Children brainstorm vessels from home and do the quick in-class version of Let us Discuss Q2–3, p.143 ("Find vessels at home that are exactly 1 litre....") using the 1-litre bottle available in class, sorting brought/imagined vessels into 'more than', 'less than', 'exactly 1 litre'. Discuss why a standard unit is more useful than a ladle or a glass for telling others how much something holds.

periods.teacher_notes: Having compared vessels informally by pouring, children are now ready to meet a named standard. The milkman discussion — why measuring cups are used when giving milk — is a strong anchor here; pose it if time allows. A common error is to think a jug always holds exactly 1 litre; press children: 'How will you check?' Tasks T-8, T-9, T-11, and T-12 provide additional reasoning practice on the lemonade picture: Let us Do Q3, Q4, Q6, Q7, p.142.
materials: Lemonade stall picture (from textbook or display)

periods.activity_title: Half and Quarter Litre: Reading and Guessing

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the picture and tick the appropriate word: the mug holds a litre/half litre; the glass holds a litre/half litre/quarter litre of water.
First guess then check with the 1 litre bottle: how much water does a bucket/mug/glass hold — more than/less than/equal to 1 litre/half litre/quarter litre.

time_bands.activity: Begin by pouring water into the 1-litre bottle to its halfway mark and its quarter mark, showing children what half litre and quarter litre look like in a familiar bottle. Ask: 'If this is 1 litre, what is this amount?' — building visual sense before the picture task.

Children work through Let us Think (a–b), p.144 ("Look at the picture and tick the appropriate word: the mug holds a litre/half litre....") individually, then compare answers with a partner. Discuss how the balance diagram in the picture lets us read the relationship without pouring.

Move into Let us Explore (a–c), p.144 ("First guess then check with the 1 litre bottle: how much water does a bucket/mug/glass hold...."). Children record their guesses, then use the 1-litre bottle to verify, filling it to full, half, or quarter as needed. Groups share whether their guesses were close, building the habit of estimating before measuring.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have worked with the litre as a whole are now meeting it as a divisible unit; the half and quarter arise from sharing, not from new rules. A common error is to think 'quarter litre' means any small amount — use the bottle to show that a quarter is exactly one of four equal parts. Encourage children to describe their guesses in words ('I think it is less than half') before reaching for the bottle.
materials: 1-litre bottle with half and quarter marks indicated
Bucket, mug, glass, and other classroom vessels
Recording sheet for guesses and results

periods.activity_title: Hands as Scales: Feeling and Comparing Weight

tasks_in_class.description: Hold listed things (lunch box & pencil box, school bag & lunch bag, apple & watermelon, balloon & basketball) in both hands in pairs; observe and record which is heavier.
Write names of objects and how many coins or erasers balance the object on a pan-balance (pencil, ping pong ball, and other self-chosen objects).
Write the names of all objects measured in the order of lightest to heaviest.

time_bands.activity: Distribute pairs of objects (lunch box and pencil box, balloon and basketball, etc.) around the class. Children do Let us Do (hand-holding activity), p.145 ("Hold listed things…observe and record which is heavier....") — each child holds one object in each hand, eyes closed, then records which side felt heavier. Whole-class check: does everyone agree?

Introduce the pan-balance. Demonstrate how it tips toward the heavier side. Children carry out Let us Do Q1, p.146 ("Write names of objects and how many coins or erasers balance the object....") in small groups, placing a pencil in one pan and adding coins one by one to the other until the pans are level, recording the count.

Using the coin/eraser counts from the balance activity, children do Let us Do (ordering), p.146 ("Write the names of all objects measured in the order of lightest to heaviest...."). Groups arrange their object names in a line from fewest coins to most, then share their ordering with the class and discuss any disagreements.

periods.teacher_notes: The hand-as-scale activity lets children build body sense of weight before any instrument appears; do not skip it in favour of going straight to the balance. A common error is to read the balance by which pan is higher rather than which is lower — the heavier side goes down. Task T-19 (matchbox activity) extends the same informal-weight idea and is suitable as additional practice: Let us Do Q2, p.146.
materials: Assorted classroom objects (pencil, ping pong ball, lunch box, pencil box)

periods.activity_title: Weight Hunt: Finding and Feeling One Kilogram

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (Weight hunt) Q1–3, p.147
tasks_in_class.description: In groups, find a bag heavier and lighter than yours; discuss why; count books to see if there is a difference; can you equalise bags by moving a book?
Can you guess which things (pencil, table, water bottle, lunch box, balloons, pillow, eraser) are likely to be lighter or heavier than 1 kilogram? Put a tick mark in the appropriate box.

homework.description: With parents' help, find objects at home on which 1 kilogram is written; feel it; write names of the objects that are 1 kilogram.

time_bands.activity: Pass around a 1 kg salt packet. Each child lifts it, holds it for a moment, and says one word to describe the feeling. Establish: this is 1 kilogram — the standard unit of weight.

Groups do the weight-hunt — Let us Do (Weight hunt) Q1–3, p.147 ("In groups, find a bag heavier and lighter than yours; discuss why; count books...."). Children compare school bags by lifting, discuss why one feels heavier, then try moving a book from the heavier bag to the lighter one and lifting again to see if they balance better.

Working individually, children complete Let us Do Q5, p.147 ("Can you guess which things are likely to be lighter or heavier than 1 kilogram?...") by ticking their guess for each listed object, then share answers. Discuss: 'How did you decide? Could you lift a table? Is a pencil heavier than the salt packet?' — connecting reasoning to the body-sense built with the packet.

periods.teacher_notes: The 1 kg salt packet is the concrete anchor for everything that follows in this section; ensure every child lifts it before the guessing task. A common error is to equate size with weight — children may tick 'pillow heavier than 1 kg' because it is large; prompt: 'Is a big pillow hard to carry?' Task T-22 goes home so children can find real kilogram-labelled packets with family support.
materials: 1 kg salt packet (or equivalent standard 1 kg mass)
Pencil, water bottle, lunch box, balloon, eraser for demonstration

periods.activity_title: Half Kilogram, Quarter Kilogram: Reading Balance Diagrams

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the balance and tick the correct word: each daal packet weighs a half kilogram/kilogram; each tea packet weighs a half kilogram/quarter kilogram/kilogram.
Look around your house; identify objects about half a kilogram and quarter of a kilogram; feel and guess; list and verify with the 1 kilogram salt packet.

time_bands.activity: Revisit the 1 kg packet. Ask: 'If I share this into two equal parts, how heavy is each part?' Establish half kilogram. Then: 'If I share into four equal parts?' Establish quarter kilogram. Show the balance diagrams in the textbook for orientation.

Children study the balance pictures and complete Let us Do Q6(a–b), p.148 ("Look at the balance and tick the correct word: each daal packet weighs a half kilogram/kilogram....") individually, reasoning from how many packets are needed to balance the 1 kg standard shown. Pairs compare and discuss any differences.

Children carry out Let us Explore, p.148 ("Look around your house; identify objects about half a kilogram and quarter of a kilogram....") adapted for the classroom — picking up objects available (pencil case, water bottle, small bag) and comparing against the 1 kg packet to judge if each is close to half or quarter. They list their estimates and any they can verify by holding both the object and a half-filled packet simultaneously.

periods.teacher_notes: Children who have felt the full kilogram are now asked to reason about its parts; the balance diagram in the book is a pictorial model of the same relationship they explored with the pan-balance when weighing with coins. A common error is to think 'half kilogram' and 'quarter kilogram' are just qualitative descriptors (heavy, light) rather than exact fractions; anchor always to 'two halves make one whole kilogram'.
materials: Assorted small classroom objects for estimation

section_titles: Tricky balls — reasoning with a pan-balance
periods.activity_title: Tricky Balls: Logic Puzzles with the Pan-Balance

tasks_in_class.description: 3 similar balls, one heavier, 2 equal; using only a pan-balance and no weights: (a) how many times will you have to weigh? (b) use the balance only once to identify the heavy ball.
Three same-sized balls of different weights (red, orange, green); using pan-balance without weights, find which is heaviest and which is lightest.

time_bands.activity: Show three similar-looking balls (or three bags of similar appearance). Tell the class: 'One of these is heavier than the other two, which are exactly equal. You have a pan-balance but no weights. How will you find the heavy one?' Allow two minutes of quiet thinking before any discussion.

Groups work on Tricky balls Q1(a–b), p.149 ("3 similar balls, one heavier, 2 equal…use the balance only once to identify the heavy ball...."). Each group discusses and agrees on a strategy, then one group demonstrates with the actual balance if available, or acts it out. Key question: 'Can you do it in one weighing? How do you know one is enough?'

Pose Tricky balls Q2, p.149 ("Three same-sized balls of different weights (red, orange, green)…find which is heaviest and which is lightest...."). Groups map out a sequence of weighings on paper, label results, and determine the order. Groups share their strategy; compare whether different sequences all work, and which takes fewer steps.

periods.teacher_notes: This section demands pure relational reasoning — no numbers, no standard weights, only the direction a balance tips. A common error in Q1 is to say 'weigh all three at once', which does not isolate the heavy ball; guide children to see that placing one ball on each side leaves the third unweighed and uses the balance's information fully. Encourage children to explain their reasoning in words before acting.
materials: Three similar-looking balls or bags (one subtly heavier)
Three differently coloured balls or markers to represent red, orange, green
Recording sheet for mapping weighing sequences

section_titles: Tricky balls — reasoning with a pan-balance
periods.activity_title: Capacity, Weight and Logic: A Chapter Consolidation

tasks_in_class.description: Tick the right name: Nita/Monu/Ritu's glass holds the most milk. Nita/Monu/Ritu's glass holds the least milk.
Which of these would you use for distributing the lemonade in glasses? Why?
How many ladles are needed to fill 4 glasses?
Fill a matchbox with sand; guess and then verify how many matchboxes balance pencil box, a spoon, 4 marbles.

time_bands.activity: Quick whole-class oral round: the teacher holds up a glass, a bowl, and a bottle and asks children to rank them by capacity using what they know about comparing vessels. Then hold up the 1-litre bottle and a small cup — which is more, less, exactly 1 litre? Children respond, giving brief reasons, consolidating the capacity ideas built across earlier units.

Children complete Let us Do Q4(a–b), p.141 ("Tick the right name: Nita/Monu/Ritu's glass holds the most milk....") and Let us Do Q4, p.142 ("Which of these would you use for distributing the lemonade in glasses? Why?...") individually, then pairs compare. The second item invites a 'why' — press children for a reason in words.

Whole class works through Let us Do Q6, p.142 ("How many ladles are needed to fill 4 glasses?..."). Children reason aloud — if 2 ladles fill 1 glass, how many for 4? — before writing the answer. This connects the informal-unit reasoning from the lemonade picture to a short multiplication-in-context problem.

Groups do Let us Do Q2, p.146 ("Fill a matchbox with sand; guess and then verify how many matchboxes balance pencil box, a spoon, 4 marbles...."), completing the guess-then-verify cycle for weight one more time with matchboxes as informal weights. Close with a brief class discussion: 'Why do we eventually need the kilogram instead of matchboxes?' — linking back to the standard-unit idea that runs through the whole chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the capacity and weight strands through tasks that have not yet been used in class, giving children a fresh application of ideas they have been building. A common error at this stage is to answer 'why' questions ('why use a jug?') with 'because it is bigger' rather than reasoning about capacity and convenience; push for answers that name the measurement idea. The closing discussion on why standard units matter is the conceptual closure of the chapter.
materials: Glass, bowl, bottle for capacity comparison

items.prompt: You have a tall thin glass and a short wide bowl. Priya says the tall glass holds more water because it is taller. Ravi says you cannot tell just by looking. Who is right? What can you do to find out?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Ravi is right. You cannot tell just by looking at shape. Pour the water from each into same-sized cups to compare how much each holds.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pour contents of each vessel into identical same-sized cups and count or compare the levels.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child act it out with real cups; stretch: ask them to find a third vessel and rank all three.

exercise.description: Get three vessels (small bowl, glass, bottle) from home; guess how many small bowls fill each; pour water from one vessel into another to check.

items.prompt: Neha uses a 1-litre bottle to check her kitchen jug. She fills the bottle once and pours it into the jug. The jug is not full yet. What does this tell her about the jug?

options.label: A
options.text: The jug and the bottle hold the same amount.

options.label: C
options.text: The jug holds less than 1 litre.

options.label: D
options.text: The jug holds more than 1 litre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The jug holds more than 1 litre, because 1 full litre bottle was not enough to fill it.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: If filling a vessel once with the standard 1-litre bottle does not fill it, the vessel holds more than 1 litre.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child thinks 'one pour' means 'exactly one litre' without checking whether the jug is full.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child has reversed the relationship — if the jug is still not full after one litre, it needs more, not less.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child has not connected the pour result to a comparison conclusion.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: demonstrate with a real bottle and a larger jug; stretch: ask how many litres the jug might hold and how they would find out.

exercise.description: Find vessels at home that are exactly 1 litre using the 1 litre bottle to check; identify vessels that are more than or less than 1 litre.

items.prompt: You have a 1-litre bottle. You want to know if your classroom mug holds more than, less than, or equal to half a litre. Describe the steps you would follow to find out.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Fill the 1-litre bottle halfway (half litre). Pour that water into the mug. If the mug overflows, it holds less than half a litre. If it is not full, it holds more. If it is exactly full, it holds half a litre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Pour exactly half the 1-litre bottle into the mug and observe whether the mug overflows, remains not full, or fills exactly.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: let the child pour and observe with real materials; stretch: ask them to then check if the mug is closer to a quarter litre or half a litre.

exercise.description: First guess then check with the 1 litre bottle: how much water does a bucket/mug/glass hold — more than/less than/equal to 1 litre/half litre/quarter litre.

items.prompt: Arjun holds a full water bottle in his right hand and an empty bottle in his left hand. His right hand feels pulled down much more. What can he say about the two bottles?

options.label: A
options.text: Both bottles are the same weight.

options.label: B
options.text: He cannot tell without a weighing scale.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The full bottle is heavier. The hand that feels more pulled down is holding the heavier object.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The hand holding the heavier object is pulled down more — the body acts as an informal balance.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Child has reversed the relationship between the feeling of pull and which object is heavier.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child has ignored the difference in sensation described in the question.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has not understood that the hands can serve as an informal comparison instrument.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: have the child hold two real objects of different weight; stretch: ask them to find a third object and rank all three by feel.

exercise.description: Hold listed things (lunch box & pencil box, school bag & lunch bag, apple & watermelon, balloon & basketball) in both hands in pairs; observe and record which is heavier.

items.prompt: You place a pencil on one side of a pan-balance and add coins one by one to the other side until the pans are level. It takes 8 coins. Then you place a ping pong ball on one side and add coins until the pans are level again. It takes 5 coins. Which object is heavier? How do you know?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The pencil is heavier. It needed 8 coins to balance it, and the ping pong ball needed only 5. More coins means more weight.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The object that needs more coins to balance it on a pan-balance is the heavier one.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: draw two balance pictures with 8 and 5 coins for the child to compare visually; stretch: ask which object they would predict is heavier before trying — a sharpener or a rubber — and how many coins they expect.

exercise.description: Write names of objects and how many coins or erasers balance the object on a pan-balance (pencil, ping pong ball, and other self-chosen objects).

items.prompt: In a weight hunt, Meena's bag feels heavier than Rani's bag. Meena has 6 books in her bag and Rani has 4 books. They move 1 book from Meena's bag to Rani's. Now Meena has 5 books and Rani has 5 books. What is most likely true now?

options.label: B
options.text: Moving one book makes no difference.

options.label: D
options.text: The bags feel closer in weight than before.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The bags feel closer in weight than before. Moving one book from the heavier bag to the lighter one reduces the difference.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Transferring an object from the heavier side reduces the gap — both bags now have equal numbers of books.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child has not connected the equalised book count with an equalised weight.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child has reversed the direction of the change — Rani gained weight but so did the bag, it does not flip to heavier.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child does not connect removing a book from one bag to a change in its weight.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: act it out with two real bags and books; stretch: ask what would happen if two books were moved instead.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (Weight hunt) Q1–3, p.147
exercise.description: In groups, find a bag heavier and lighter than yours; discuss why; count books to see if there is a difference; can you equalise bags by moving a book?

items.prompt: Siya picks up a packet of rice from her kitchen. It says 500 g on the label. She also picks up a small packet of tea that says 250 g. She has a 1 kg salt packet to compare with. Is the rice packet more than, less than, or equal to half a kilogram? Is the tea packet more than, less than, or equal to a quarter kilogram?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The rice packet (500 g) is equal to half a kilogram, because half of 1000 g is 500 g. The tea packet (250 g) is equal to a quarter kilogram, because a quarter of 1000 g is 250 g.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Half of 1 kilogram is 500 g and a quarter of 1 kilogram is 250 g; compare the label number to these.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: show the child the 1 kg packet and physically fold the idea of halving and quartering; stretch: ask how many tea packets would balance the rice packet.

exercise.description: Look around your house; identify objects about half a kilogram and quarter of a kilogram; feel and guess; list and verify with the 1 kilogram salt packet.

items.prompt: Three children pour their drinks into same-sized cups to compare. Anu's drink fills 3 cups, Benu's fills 2 cups, and Chand's fills 4 cups. Who drank the least?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Benu drank the least — her drink filled only 2 same-sized cups, which is fewer than Anu's 3 and Chand's 4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compare the number of same-sized cups each drink fills; the fewest cups means the least liquid.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child may have confused 'least' with the middle value rather than the smallest.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child has identified the most rather than the least.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child has not used the cup-count information to distinguish the amounts.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: draw three rows of cups and count; stretch: ask by how many cups Chand drank more than Benu.

exercise.description: Who drank the most milk? Who drank the least milk? (from the picture of three glasses poured into same-sized glasses)

items.prompt: At a lemonade stall, it takes 3 ladles to fill 1 bowl and 2 bowls to fill 1 jug. How many ladles does it take to fill the jug? Show your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 6 ladles. 3 ladles fill 1 bowl, and 2 bowls fill the jug, so 3 × 2 = 6 ladles fill the jug.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of ladles per bowl by the number of bowls per jug.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: draw the chain — 3 ladles → 1 bowl, 1 bowl → half jug — and count; stretch: ask how many ladles would fill 3 jugs.

exercise.description: How many ladles fill the bowl? How many glasses can be filled by the jug? (from the lemonade stall picture)

items.prompt: Nita fills a 1-litre bottle completely and pours it all into a bowl. The bowl is full and there is water left over in the bottle. What does this tell us about the bowl?

options.label: B
options.text: The bowl holds half a litre.

options.label: C
options.text: The bowl holds less than 1 litre.

options.label: D
options.text: The bowl holds more than 1 litre.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The bowl holds less than 1 litre. The bowl became full before all the water was poured out, so it cannot hold a full litre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: If the vessel fills before the standard 1-litre bottle is empty, the vessel holds less than 1 litre.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child has not noticed that the bowl filled before the bottle was empty.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child has reversed the relationship — if the bowl overflows, it cannot hold more.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has guessed a specific sub-unit without any evidence; the pour only tells us 'less than 1 litre', not exactly how much.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: demonstrate with a real bottle and bowl; stretch: ask what additional step would tell us if the bowl is closer to half or quarter litre.

exercise.description: Tick the appropriate word: the glass holds more than/less than 1 litre; the bowl holds more than/less than 1 litre; the jug holds more than/less than/exactly 1 litre.

items.prompt: Look at the picture in your book. The mug is shown balanced with water that is exactly half the 1-litre bottle. The glass is shown balanced with water that is exactly one quarter of the 1-litre bottle. Which statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: The glass holds more than the mug.

options.label: B
options.text: The mug and glass hold the same amount.

options.label: C
options.text: The mug holds a full litre.

options.label: D
options.text: The mug holds more than the glass.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The mug holds more than the glass. Half a litre is greater than a quarter litre.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Half of 1 litre is greater than a quarter of 1 litre, so the mug holds more.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Child has reversed the comparison of half and quarter.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has not distinguished between half and quarter litre.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child has confused 'half litre' with 'full litre'.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: mark half and quarter on a bottle for the child to see; stretch: ask how many glasses of water would fill the mug.

exercise.description: Look at the picture and tick the appropriate word: the mug holds a litre/half litre; the glass holds a litre/half litre/quarter litre of water.

items.prompt: After weighing four objects on a pan-balance using coins, a class found: a rubber needs 3 coins, a pencil needs 7 coins, a sharpener needs 5 coins, a crayon needs 4 coins. Write these objects in order from lightest to heaviest.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rubber (3), crayon (4), sharpener (5), pencil (7) — from lightest to heaviest.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Order the objects by the number of coins needed to balance them; fewer coins means lighter.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: write the coin numbers below the object names and count up; stretch: ask how many more coins the heaviest needs than the lightest.

exercise.description: Write the names of all objects measured in the order of lightest to heaviest.

items.prompt: A pencil, a table, a water bottle, and a balloon are placed one at a time on a pan-balance against a 1 kg salt packet. Which object is most likely to make the balance tip toward the salt packet side?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The water bottle. A full water bottle is the closest in weight to 1 kg among the choices; a pencil and balloon are far lighter, and a table is far heavier.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The salt packet side tips down when the object in the other pan is lighter than 1 kg; of the options, the water bottle is closest to but still less than 1 kg.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has not considered that a pencil is far lighter than 1 kg.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Child has confused 'heavier than 1 kg' with 'makes the salt packet side tip down' — if the table is heavier, the table side would tip down, not the salt packet side.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child has not considered that a balloon is far lighter than 1 kg.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: have the child hold the salt packet and then a pencil to feel the difference; stretch: ask which objects would make the balance tip toward the object rather than the salt packet.

exercise.description: Can you guess which things (pencil, table, water bottle, lunch box, balloons, pillow, eraser) are likely to be lighter or heavier than 1 kilogram? Put a tick mark in the appropriate box.

items.prompt: A balance picture shows 2 daal packets on one side and 1 kg on the other side, and the pans are level. What does each daal packet weigh? Write how you know.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each daal packet weighs half a kilogram. Because 2 packets together equal 1 kg, each packet is 1 kg divided equally into 2, which is half a kilogram.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: If 2 equal packets balance 1 kg, each packet weighs 1 kg ÷ 2 = half a kilogram.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: fold a strip of paper to show halving; stretch: ask how many daal packets would balance 2 kg.

exercise.description: Look at the balance and tick the correct word: each daal packet weighs a half kilogram/kilogram; each tea packet weighs a half kilogram/quarter kilogram/kilogram.

items.section_title: Tricky balls — reasoning with a pan-balance
items.prompt: You have 3 balls that look the same. Two balls weigh the same, but one is heavier. You have a pan-balance and no weights. Describe what you would do in ONE weighing to find the heavy ball.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Place one ball on the left pan and one ball on the right pan. If the balance tips, the lower pan holds the heavy ball. If the pans are level, the ball not placed on the balance is the heavy one.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place one ball on each side; the side that tips down holds the heavier ball, or if level, the unused ball is the heavy one.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: act it out with labelled bags; stretch: ask whether this strategy would still work with 4 balls (one heavier) and one weighing.

exercise.description: 3 similar balls, one heavier, 2 equal; using only a pan-balance and no weights: (a) how many times will you have to weigh? (b) use the balance only once to identify the heavy ball.

items.section_title: Tricky balls — reasoning with a pan-balance
items.prompt: You have a red ball, an orange ball, and a green ball. They look the same but weigh differently. You use a pan-balance (no weights). First you weigh red against orange — red is heavier. Then you weigh orange against green — orange is heavier. Without any more weighing, write the order of the balls from lightest to heaviest.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Green is the lightest, then orange, then red. From the first weighing: red is heavier than orange. From the second weighing: orange is heavier than green. So the order lightest to heaviest is: green, orange, red.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Chain the two comparison results: green < orange < red, giving the full order without a third weighing.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: draw arrows showing red > orange > green and read the chain; stretch: ask whether a third weighing (red against green) would be needed to confirm and why.

exercise.description: Three same-sized balls of different weights (red, orange, green); using pan-balance without weights, find which is heaviest and which is lightest.

items.prompt: Asha's cup holds more water than Bina's cup. Bina's cup holds more water than Charu's cup. Fill in the blank: Asha's cup holds ___ water than Charu's cup.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: More. Asha > Bina > Charu, so Asha holds more than Charu.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Follow the comparison chain: if A > B and B > C, then A > C.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Child has reversed the direction of the comparison.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Child has not tracked the transitive relationship across three cups.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Child does not recognise that the two statements together give enough information.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: draw three cups in a line with arrows showing more-than; stretch: ask the child to write a sentence comparing Bina's and Charu's cups.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks with 'more' or 'less': Nita's glass holds ___ milk than Monu's; Monu's holds ___ than Nita's; Ritu's holds ___ than Nita's.

items.prompt: At a lemonade stall, 1 jug holds enough lemonade to fill 4 glasses. How many glasses can be filled using 5 jugs of lemonade?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 20 glasses. 5 jugs × 4 glasses per jug = 20 glasses.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of jugs by the number of glasses each jug fills.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: draw 5 jugs and write 4 under each, then add; stretch: ask how many jugs are needed to fill exactly 24 glasses.

exercise.description: How many glasses can be filled with 3 jugs of lemonade?

items.prompt: It takes 3 ladles to fill 1 glass. How many ladles are needed to fill 6 glasses?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 18 ladles. 6 glasses × 3 ladles per glass = 18 ladles.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the number of glasses by the number of ladles needed to fill each glass.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Struggling: draw 6 glasses and write 3 ladles under each, then count all ladles; stretch: ask how many ladles are needed if each glass only needs 2 ladles instead of 3.

exercise.description: How many ladles are needed to fill 4 glasses?
